einzeiler: Novelist Adrienne Brodeur on family myths, writing fiction, and her novel Little Monsters.
kurzfassung: Novelist and editor Adrienne Brodeur discusses her journey from the literary magazine world to writing memoir and fiction. She shares insights into the complex dynamics of sibling relationships and parental figures depicted in her book Little Monsters. The conversation also touches on her writing process, character development, and upcoming creative projects.
stichpunkte: Discussion of Cape Cod's profound influence as a setting and constant presence in her life and writing
Transition from working behind the scenes as a book editor and literary magazine curator to writing her own stories
The experience of publishing Melissa Bank's foundational early stories through the literary magazine Zoetrope All-Story
Comparing the emotional honesty of fiction versus the constraints of protecting real people in memoir
The structural inspiration drawn from the story of Cain and Abel for shaping family dynamics in Little Monsters
Developing morally complicated characters like Ken and addressing mental health dynamics through the character Adam
Adapting Little Monsters into a screenplay and the unique challenge of condensing a novel into dialogue-driven scenes
Plans for launching a Substack newsletter focused on unexpected human connections sparked through books

beschreibung:
Description:
Some families run on rules nobody ever wrote down. Here is your role. Here is what we talk about. Here is who gets forgiven and who gets blamed. We accept those terms as children, and then one day we look up and wonder who exactly signed us up for the job.
August’s Jen Hatmaker Book Club pick is Little Monsters, and Adrienne Brodeur came with the whole story behind it. She spent thirty years on the other side of the pen, co-founding Zoetrope: All-Story with Francis Ford Coppola, editing at HMH Books, judging the National Book Award, and now running Aspen Words. She published one novel of her own in 2005, then waited fourteen years for the next book, a memoir that broke a silence she had kept since she was fourteen.
Adrienne and Jen get into the unspoken rules every family runs on, why estrangement takes love rather than indifference, and what Cain and Abel taught her about the gifts we give our parents. Adrienne explains why fiction can feel more honest than memoir, makes an unpopular case for Ken, and talks about writing mania with compassion rather than spectacle. Plus the stack of books a stepmother handed her that redirected her whole life, the screenplay she is writing, and the book club’s standing offer to cast the movie.
***
Thought-provoking Quotes:
He’s wounded, and wounded people wound. – Adrienne Brodeur
Understanding someone isn’t quite the same as absolving them. – Adrienne Brodeur
Fiction can sometimes feel more honest than memoir. I don’t mean factual honesty. I mean emotionally unguarded. – Adrienne Brodeur
Who the hell decided that peacemaker was my job, or golden child, or secret keeper, or difficult one? – Adrienne Brodeur
Turns out dead mothers still have an excellent work ethic. – Adrienne Brodeur
Everyone wanted a flat version of themselves. – Jen Hatmaker
We have family stories that we’re telling too, even believing, that we’re trying to believe. – Jen Hatmaker
Some of our characters landed on their feet, but they landed on their feet in a different zip code. – Jen Hatmaker
